source: de Kleer and Williams (1987) Diagnosing multiple faults, Artificial Intelligence 32(1):97-130
finding: GDE (General Diagnostic Engine) picks the next measurement by a minimum-entropy rule: the best probe is the one that minimises the expected entropy of the candidate probabilities after the measurement. Expected entropy is computed from the current candidate probabilities and the outcome sets each probe would induce. Could not open the PDF this session (host would not resolve; local copy was not a PDF). Content here comes from search-result excerpts and from later papers that restate it.
numbers: none verified first-hand
limits: Second-hand. Re-read the primary text before citing formulas. Prior fault probabilities are assumed independent per component.
agent_relevance: This is the founding rule for S7-style probe choice: score each candidate test by expected remaining entropy over surviving hypotheses, computed in code.

source: Siddiqi and Huang (2010) New Advances in Sequential Diagnosis, AAAI-10 / KR workshop copy
finding: Restates GDE: it picks measurement points by reducing the entropy over a computed set of diagnoses (minimum-cardinality or leading diagnoses). This breaks when the diagnosis set is huge. Using only a few probable diagnoses scales, but raises the chance of irrelevant measurements and raises average diagnostic cost (de Kleer 1992). Diagnostic cost is defined as the number of measurements.
numbers: Cost = number of measurements. Benchmarks: ISCAS-85 circuits, plus 50 subcircuits of size 13-16 and 10 of size 17, each with 5 single-, 5 double-, 5 triple-fault scenarios.
quote: focusing on a smaller set of probable diagnoses scales the approach but can increase the likelihood of irrelevant measurements
limits: Their own tutorial GDE only held minimal diagnoses and could not solve any full ISCAS-85 circuit.
agent_relevance: Shows the central trade: scoring probes over all hypotheses is best but costly; scoring over a short list is cheap but wastes probes. An LLM agent can only hold a short list, so expect this penalty.

source: Siddiqi and Huang (2010) New Advances in Sequential Diagnosis
finding: Heuristic H1: measure the variable with maximal Shannon entropy over its own outcomes. This alone worked badly in early tests because many unlikely diagnoses distort the information estimate. Fix A: prune diagnoses with more than k faults. Fix B (used): first pick the component with the highest posterior failure probability, then measure the highest-entropy variable of that component. Fix B gave a similar gain without needing to know k.
numbers: Table 2, circuit c432 (160 gates), no pruning: single-fault random order 92.3 measurements, entropy-of-wires only 42.0, failure-probability plus entropy 6.7; five-fault random 117.8, failure-probability plus entropy 9.4. c880 five-fault: random 306.4, failure-probability plus entropy 15.8. Random strategy used the same d-DNNF stopping test.
quote: We select a component that has the highest posterior probability of failure ... and then ... measure the one that has the highest entropy.
limits: Combines two heuristics. Gate-level circuits, noise-free observations, faults injected at random.
agent_relevance: Raw entropy alone is a weak probe rule when the hypothesis list has junk. Pairing 'most suspect component' with 'most informative test on it' cut cost by about an order of magnitude versus random.

source: Siddiqi and Huang (2010) New Advances in Sequential Diagnosis
finding: Against GDE on small circuits the compiled approach (sdc) matched GDE in diagnostic cost but ran thousands of times faster.
numbers: Table 1: size 13 single-fault GDE 3.6 vs sdc 3.6 measurements; size 16 double-fault 3.5 vs 3.3; size 17 double-fault GDE 4.6 vs sdc 4.2 (time 4103 s vs 0.01 s).
limits: Small subcircuits, one test vector per fault scenario, 15 scenarios per circuit.
agent_relevance: Probe count can be near equal while compute differs hugely; spend tokens on the probe rule, not on full enumeration.

source: Siddiqi and Huang (2011) Sequential Diagnosis by Abstraction, JAIR 41:329-365
finding: Journal version. States that an optimal sequential diagnosis is a policy (a plan of measurements conditioned on earlier outcomes, Heckerman et al. 1995), that computing it is intractable, and that practice uses a heuristic: Shannon entropy (formula 3) over the probability of diagnoses. Adds a measurement heuristic that needs no diagnosis list once the system is a Bayesian network compiled to d-DNNF, plus abstraction to scale.
numbers: Same GDE comparison: 50 circuits of size 13-16 and 10 of size 17; scales to all ISCAS-85 circuits except one flat circuit.
quote: As computing optimal policies is intractable in general, we follow the approach of heuristic measurement point selection
limits: Combinational circuits with a given probabilistic model; no measurement costs (cost = count).
agent_relevance: Confirms the standard framing: optimal policy is out of reach, one-step entropy heuristic is the working compromise.

source: Siddiqi and Huang (2011) Sequential Diagnosis by Abstraction
finding: Reports de Kleer (2006) studied how sensitive diagnostic cost is to the 'policy' used to estimate posterior probabilities of diagnoses in GDE's heuristic. Their own method's cost can also depend on the starting probability model; sensitivity analysis was left open.
numbers: none
quote: our algorithm can be sensitive to the initial probabilistic model given
limits: Only a pointer to de Kleer 2006; not opened.
agent_relevance: Probe choice is only as good as the prior over hypotheses; a wrong prior from an LLM would mis-rank probes. Treat priors as uncertain.

source: Breese and Heckerman (1996) Decision-Theoretic Troubleshooting: A Framework for Repair and Experiment (UAI)
finding: Extends diagnosis to cost-weighted action. Under single-fault, independent-component, observe-then-repair assumptions, the minimum expected cost sequence orders components by decreasing p_i / C_io (probability the component is the fault divided by cost to observe it). Proven by swapping any two adjacent steps. Unobservable components fit the same rule with cost of repair. The planner is used myopically: estimate the expected repair cost of three plan classes, pick the next action, update probabilities, repeat.
numbers: Rule: order by p_i/C_io descending; under single fault sum p_i = 1. Three plan classes: repair in sequence, gather evidence then repair, change configuration then observe then repair.
quote: the minimum expected cost sequence is obtained by ordering the components according to a decreasing probability to cost ratio
limits: Single-fault and independence assumptions; optimal plan overall is intractable; the paper only approximates it.
agent_relevance: A cost-weighted probe rule we can code: rank checks by P(suspect is the fault) divided by cost to check it. Cheap checks on likely suspects go first.

source: Heckerman, Breese, Rommelse (1995) Decision-theoretic troubleshooting, Communications of the ACM 38(3):49-57
finding: Source of the p/C ordering and of choosing the next repair or observation by estimated expected repair cost with a Bayesian network. Cited by Siddiqi and Huang for the 'test the most likely failing component' idea and for the warning that the single-fault heuristic can hurt in multiple-fault cases. Only the abstract page and citing papers were seen.
numbers: none first-hand
limits: Not opened. Siddiqi and Huang report the authors said the single-fault assumption could compromise cost with multiple faults.
agent_relevance: Cost-ratio probing assumes one fault; with several faults the ordering can be wrong.

source: Golovin and Krause (2011) Adaptive Submodularity: Theory and Applications in Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization, JAIR 42
finding: Defines adaptive submodularity and proves that a myopic adaptive greedy policy is near-optimal when the objective has that property. Covers sensor placement, viral marketing and Bayesian active learning, and recovers known results for generalized binary search (the splitting algorithm). Adds lazy evaluation to speed greedy probe scoring, and data-dependent bounds on the optimum.
numbers: Classic non-adaptive greedy under submodularity gets at least (1 - 1/e) of the best size-k set; tight unless P = NP (as cited in the paper).
quote: a simple adaptive greedy algorithm is guaranteed to be competitive with the optimal policy
limits: Guarantee needs adaptive monotone submodularity of the objective and an exactly known prior; robustness to a wrong prior is listed as open.
agent_relevance: Theory behind 'one-step lookahead is pretty good'. Greedy probing is safe when a probe's value does not grow with earlier probes and the prior is right.

source: Golovin and Krause (2011) Adaptive Submodularity, section on generalized binary search
finding: Half-split is the special case. Generalized binary search (GBS, the splitting algorithm) picks the query that most evenly splits the version space. Worst case it minimises the count of hypotheses agreeing with the answer; Bayesian it minimises the prior mass on the larger side. Worst-case number of queries is an O(log |H|) approximation (Arkin et al. 1993). Expected number is an O(log(1 / min_h p(h))) approximation (Kosaraju et al. 1999, Dasgupta 2004). Running GBS on a modified prior max(p(h), 1/|H|^2 log|H|) gives O(log |H|).
numbers: Approximation factors O(log|H|) worst case and O(log(1/min p)) expected; modified prior floor 1/|H|^2 log|H|.
quote: these policies myopically attempt to shrink a measure of the version space
limits: Noise-free binary outcomes; extended by Guillory and Bilmes (2009) to more labels and by Nowak (2009) to noisy answers (cited, not opened).
agent_relevance: Safe rule for the agent: if probes give clean yes/no answers, pick the one that cuts hypothesis mass nearest half. Rare hypotheses are the risk; a floor on tiny priors fixes the bound.

source: Golovin and Krause (2011) Adaptive Submodularity
finding: Kosaraju et al. (1999) call a policy progressive if every query eliminates at least one hypothesis; the GBS bound proof uses this property. Golovin and Krause use it to link greedy probing to the optimal decision tree problem.
numbers: none
limits: Optimal decision tree is hard in general; Kosaraju et al. not opened.
agent_relevance: Simple check for the agent: a chosen probe should be able to remove at least one candidate, or be dropped.

source: Rainforth, Foster, Ivanova, Bickford Smith (2023) Modern Bayesian Experimental Design, Statistical Science
finding: Defines expected information gain (EIG) of a design as the expected gain over outcomes, equal to the mutual information between parameters and outcome, traceable to Lindley (1956). In sequential use, EIG for step t is computed given the history of earlier designs and outcomes. Classic Bayesian adaptive design is myopic and needs a model update at each step, often too slow. Newer deep adaptive design learns a policy that can be non-myopic and runs in a forward pass.
numbers: none
quote: the traditional BAD approach ... is actually subtly sub-optimal because it makes greedy, myopic, decisions
limits: Review; claims that deep adaptive design beats greedy come from cited papers, not retested here.
agent_relevance: Names the exact quantity we compute when scoring probes. Also says one-step EIG misses plans where an early cheap probe sets up a later strong one.

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas (2023) Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models (GATE)
finding: LMs prompted to ask open-ended questions, yes/no questions, or to generate edge cases elicited human preferences better than user-written prompts or labelled examples in two of three domains. Pool-based active learning did not beat GATE in content recommendation. Users found interactive elicitation less mentally demanding than writing prompts.
numbers: 388 participants on Prolific across email validation, content recommendation, moral reasoning. Metric: area under p(correct) vs interaction time. Significance versus baselines only in content recommendation and email validation. Average entropy of p(yes) across participants per question: 0.77 bits.
limits: Humans answer; no explicit entropy computation in the main LM methods (LM just asked to be informative). No significance in the moral domain.
agent_relevance: An LM can ask useful questions without an entropy calculator, but the gain is small and domain dependent. Supports scoring in code rather than trusting the LM's sense of what is informative.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing Experiments and Revising Rules with Natural Language and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: LLM proposes hypotheses (natural-language rules) and candidate experiments; the program keeps a particle belief over hypotheses and picks the experiment by expected information gain. In Zendo, information-gain reranking beat both an LLM that picks experiments by prompt and a random generator. Score is average predictive posterior accuracy over 8 test scenes.
numbers: Table 3 (fuzzy rules / hard rules): LLM-chosen experiments 4.52 / 4.72; random 5.03 / 5.84; InfoGain 5.35 / 6.55. Humans averaged 5.26 of 8. 5 seeds, standard errors about 0.08 to 0.19.
quote: an LLM--on its own--does not generate experiments that are as effective
limits: Small synthetic domain; 10 rules; human data from 30 participants x 10 games (Bramley et al. 2018).
agent_relevance: Strongest in-domain test: the LLM prompted to choose its own probe is worse than a random one; scoring by expected information gain in code wins. Matches schema rule G5 (code selects).

source: Piriyakulkij et al. (2024) Doing Experiments and Revising Rules
finding: Who generates candidates matters less than the selection rule. A hand-built random proposer reranked by information gain performed about the same as an LLM proposer reranked by information gain. More candidates helped: 1, 5, 10 candidates.
numbers: Table 4, online hard-rule model, Zendo: random proposer 5.84 / 6.23 / 6.55 (+/- 0.19 / 0.16 / 0.28); LLM proposer 5.73 / 6.19 / 6.55 (+/- 0.16 / 0.12 / 0.13) at 1 / 5 / 10 candidates.
quote: a random proposer, hand-designed under reasonable assumptions, performs similarly to an LLM experiment proposer
limits: Single domain; the random proposer was hand-designed for Zendo.
agent_relevance: Budget lever: generate about 10 candidate probes cheaply, then rank by computed information gain. Going from 1 to 10 candidates gained about 0.7 of 8 scenes.

source: Piriyakulkij et al. (2024) Doing Experiments and Revising Rules
finding: On ActiveACRE (causal blicket task with 7 experiments), online inference with hard rules solved more whole tasks than batch inference or batch with refinement. Authors report LLMs are good at proposing and revising hypotheses but do not consistently beat random guessing at proposing experiments.
numbers: Task-solving: online hard rules 0.35 +/- 0.11 vs batch hard 0.15 +/- 0.08 and batch with refinement 0.10 +/- 0.07 (table layout garbled; alignment inferred). 20 tasks. ROC AUC 0.87 for the online hard model.
quote: do not consistently outperform random guessing when proposing experiments
limits: Only 20 tasks, wide error bars; row-to-method alignment inferred.
agent_relevance: Interleave probe, update, probe again; do not batch all probes up front.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT lets the LLM propose questions and simulate answers, builds a tree of possible answer paths, then rewards each question by expected information gain over a set of candidate possibilities. For a yes/no question splitting candidates into an affirmative and a negative part, information gain equals the binary entropy of the split, so a half-half split scores highest. This is the half-split rule written as entropy. Rewards are propagated up the tree to choose the question.
numbers: Equation 9: IG_v(X) = -pA log pA - pN log pN, where pA and pN are the probabilities of a yes and a no. Simulation depth limited to three steps for cost.
limits: Needs an explicit finite candidate set; assumes answers rule candidates in or out cleanly (the paper admits 'I do not have a fever' does not rule out 100%).
agent_relevance: A concrete formula our code can compute once the agent lists candidates. Shows why LLM probing needs an explicit candidate set.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts
finding: Measured gains over direct prompting (DP) on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis (DX, MedDG) and troubleshooting (FloDial), across five LLMs. Headline: success rate up 38.1 percent on average over DP.
numbers: Average gain over DP 38.1 (unit ambiguous); Llama3-70B +46.6; over CoT-SC +33.8; over Reflexion +29.9; over Original-ToT +28.3; over Adapted-ToT +12.4. Appendix tables: DX 97.0 vs 89.4 DP; MedDG 87.9 vs 74.9; FloDial 67.8 vs 42.5 (model row assumed GPT-4). Llama 3: DX 90.1 vs 80.1; FloDial 46.4 vs 29.9. Paired t-tests p < 0.05 for all rows shown.
limits: Unit of the 38.1 figure is unclear. Closed-set (CS) setting gives the candidate list; open-set is weaker. Simulated patients and answerers are LLMs.
agent_relevance: Measured gain from information-gain scoring for diagnostic question choice: about 7 to 25 points on GPT-4, largest on troubleshooting, our closest case.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts
finding: In 20 Questions closed set, UoT beat the best baseline Reflexion by an average 4.3 points; open set it beat Adapted-ToT by an average 8.7 points. CoT and PP prompting were worse than plain GPT-4 in closed-set 20 Questions. Medical conversations got shorter: on DX GPT-4 mean questions 2.0 vs 3.5 and 3.0 for DP methods. Troubleshooting FloDial: GPT-4 43.7 to 67.3 success, 7.8 questions.
numbers: 20Q: +4.3 over Reflexion (CS), +8.7 over Adapted-ToT (OS). DX questions 2.0 vs 3.5/3.0. Troubleshooting 43.7 to 67.3 success.
limits: Success is judged with an LLM-simulated answerer; entity sets are fixed lists.
agent_relevance: Structured reasoning prompts alone (CoT) did not help question choice; a scoring rule did.

source: Choudhury, Williamson, Golinski, Miao, Bickford Smith, Kirchhof, Zhang, Rainforth (2026) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design (ICLR 2026)
finding: Picks questions by expected information gain (EIG) computed from the LLM's predictive distributions, with a belief state of sampled hypotheses updated each turn. Against direct prompting it adds 37.4 percentage points on average in 20 Questions across LLMs and target sets, more than doubling success in over half of setups, never lowering it.
numbers: +37.4 percentage points average vs Prompt-Only. 3 problem sets (Animals, Celebrities, Things) of 100 targets each. LLMs: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Llama-3.3-70B, Mistral-Large, Qwen2.5-72B. Example cells: Qwen2.5-72B 32 +/- 4.7 up to 62 +/- 4.9.
limits: Targets are not given to the LLM, so the hypothesis set comes from the LLM itself; answerer was an LLM. Table column labels were lost in extraction, so per-method cells are not matched to methods.
agent_relevance: Up-to-date measured gain: code-computed EIG over sampled hypotheses roughly doubles success compared with asking the model to pick a good question.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM
finding: Separates marginal predictive entropy from true EIG. Earlier LLM question-asking work (Hu 2024, Piriyakulkij 2024, Mazzaccara 2024, Kobalczyk 2025) assumes answers are deterministic given the hidden target, which collapses EIG to marginal entropy of the answer, i.e. the Split / half-split rule. When answers are noisy or ambiguous, high marginal entropy can mean a useless question; EIG subtracts the expected conditional entropy. Their own Split baseline already beat numbers reported in earlier papers.
numbers: Four ablations (including Entropy-only and Data-Estimation). Entropy-only fails on questions with noisy answers.
limits: Ablation numbers not extracted cleanly. In preference elicitation (200 profiles, movie scores 1-5) the gain is smaller because Prompt-Only is a stronger baseline there.
agent_relevance: Key boundary: half-split is right for clean tests; when a probe's result is ambiguous (a model's judgement, a flaky test), subtract answer noise or the probe wastes a turn.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM
finding: Gains hold when the questioner and answerer are different models, and the benefit is largest when they belong to different model classes. In preference elicitation BED-LLM gave higher-rated film recommendations than Prompt-Only, a smaller boost than in 20 Questions.
numbers: Mismatch pairs: Q GPT-4o-mini with A Qwen2.5-72B, and the reverse. Preference setting: 200 profiles.
limits: Exact preference-task numbers not read from the table.
agent_relevance: Probe scoring survives a mismatch between the agent's model of the world and reality, so long as the belief update uses real outputs.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Models were tested at picking the one question that makes an underspecified problem solvable (a CSP with one missing variable). Models do well on math (GSM-Q, GSME-Q) and badly on logic and planning. Ability to solve the fully specified problem did not predict ability to pick the right question.
numbers: Over 80 percent on GSM-Q and GSME-Q; under 50 percent on Logic-Q and Planning-Q (abstract: 40-50). Models include o1-preview, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, Gemini Flash Thinking, Gemma 2 2B-27B. Zero-shot, CoT and four-shot settings.
quote: models struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version
limits: Multiple choice with one sufficient question; no costs, no noise; table layout garbled so per-model cells not used.
agent_relevance: Unaided LLMs often choose the wrong clarifying probe on logic and planning problems. Do not trust their picks; compute them.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench
finding: Accuracy fell with number of variables, number of constraints and backward-search depth, with moderate negative Spearman correlations, significant for most models in Logic-Q. Planning-Q showed weak or no correlation with those factors.
numbers: Spearman rank correlations in Table 3 (p < 0.05 marked); a breadth-first-search solver was used as reference.
limits: Exact coefficients not extracted.
agent_relevance: Probe choice gets harder as the hypothesis set grows, so the larger the set, the more the agent needs code-side scoring.

source: Siddiqi and Huang (2010) New Advances in Sequential Diagnosis
finding: Related-work note: the idea of testing the most likely failing component comes from Heckerman, Breese, Rommelse (1995), where testing a component was one unit step and the heuristic assumed a single fault. Siddiqi and Huang test each variable of a component as a unit and need no single-fault assumption. Also cites 'One step lookahead is pretty good' by de Kleer, Raiman and Shirley (1992).
numbers: none
limits: de Kleer, Raiman, Shirley 1992 not opened.
agent_relevance: Names the paper to read next on whether one-step lookahead loses much against deeper lookahead in diagnosis.

source: de Kleer, Raiman, Shirley (1992) One step lookahead is pretty good, in Readings in Model-Based Diagnosis
finding: Reported by Siddiqi and Huang as the study showing that focusing on a smaller set of probable diagnoses is cheaper but raises average diagnostic cost, and that more diagnoses aid the accuracy of the entropy heuristic. Title claims one-step lookahead is close to what deeper lookahead gives. Not opened.
numbers: none
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: If it holds, a one-step rule is good enough for the schema's probe selector; read the original to confirm.

source: Siddiqi and Huang (2011) Sequential Diagnosis by Abstraction
finding: Entropy is maximal when outcomes are equally likely and minimal when one has probability 1. In GDE the entropy is taken over the distribution of diagnoses, which is hard to compute when diagnoses are many (de Kleer and Williams 1987; de Kleer 2006).
numbers: Formula 3: H(X) = - sum Pr(X = x_i) log Pr(X = x_i).
quote: this entropy can be difficult to compute when the number of diagnoses is large
limits: Definition only.
agent_relevance: Spec of the score the agent's code should compute: entropy over its hypothesis list, before and after each candidate probe.

source: Hyafil and Rivest (1976) Constructing optimal binary decision trees is NP-complete, Information Processing Letters 5(1)
finding: Building the minimum expected-depth decision tree for testing is NP-complete, which is why practice uses greedy half-split or entropy rules. Known from standard citation in the decision-tree and active learning literature; the paper itself was not opened.
numbers: none
limits: Not opened; not seen in any text read this session.
agent_relevance: Justifies greedy probing in the schema rather than searching for the best probe sequence.
